items.title: They belong to Jerusalem’s past and present: meet the African Palestinians
items.summary:
Despite militarisation, occupation and marginalisation, African culture prevails in the Old City, something I discovered first-hand when I visited

  • Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

In occupied East Jerusalem, I met an often overlooked community: African Palestinians. This week, I explore their unique history, and how they are, in a classic diaspora fashion, integrated and marginalised in equal measure.

There are about 450 African Palestinian people in occupied East Jerusalem, mostly living in the historical buildings of the Old City, near al-Aqsa mosque. That mosque, the third holiest site in Islam after those in Mecca and Medina, is the reason they are there. While Christians make up a small part of the African Palestinian population, most African Palestinians descended from Muslim pilgrims who came to East Jerusalem in the early 20th century (before Israeli occupation), and stayed either to tend to the mosque, or to continue Islamic practice and devotion within the city’s religious ecosystem.

Continue reading...

items.title: Church in India mourns passing of beloved archbishop, a force for peace and reconciliation
items.summary:
MUMBAI – The Catholic Church in India lost a senior prelate on Wednesday, who was a prominent figure on the national stage despite his dislike of the limelight, and a force for reconciliation in the country’s troubled northeast for many decades.

Archbishop Thomas Menamparampil, a member of the Salesians of Don Bosco, died in the early hours of Wednesday, Nov. 25, at AIG Hospital, Hyderabad, of complications following a liver illness. He was 90 years old.

Cardinal Oswald Gracias, emeritus of Mumbai, told Crux Now Menamprampil was “a fearless bridge-builder” who worked tirelessly for peace, reconciliation, and Christian unity.

“He never sought to get attention to himself,” Gracias said. “He always stayed out of the center. He didn’t draw attention to it, but he did all the work.”

The 81-year-old cardinal had known the late archbishop since they were both young priests, and they worked together for many decades.

Gracias especially recalled Menamparampil’s courageous work for peace and understanding in the northeast Indian state of Manipur, where religious identity intersects with deep-rooted and complex ethnic, social, and economic conflicts.

A statement from the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of India recalled Menamparampil’s many successful efforts to bring relief to those suffering the effects violence and foster reconciliation.

The CBCI and Gracias remember Menamparampil as a frank and tireless advocate for Christians of all denominations and a respected voice capable of engaging Hindus and Muslims as an honest broker in disputes between those communities.…
items.t: Church in India mourns passing of beloved archbishop, a force for peace and reconciliation

items.title: Leo sets theologians to work on one theme with two faces
items.summary:
Pope Leo XIV has assigned two major topics to the International Theological Commission (ITC), which he received in audience on Wednesday, November 25, at the Apostolic Palace: Apostolic Tradition, and the cultural forms through which faith is transmitted across generations and cultures. The assignment comes weeks after Leo named 24 new members to the ITC on October 19. Speaking to the commission shortly before his weekly general audience, the Pope outlined the work that will occupy them over the next five years: two major themes rather than the three that have been standard in recent mandates. The first theme is Apostolic Tradition: the transmission of Christ’s message through the apostles and the Church that followed them. items.title: Spain’s World Cup hero to receive faith-sharing prize
items.summary:
Ferran Torres, the scorer of Spain’s winning goal in the 2026 World Cup final, has been given an award for the public display of his Catholic faith.

Spain’s Asociación Católica de Propagandistas (ACdP), through its Fundación Universitaria San Pablo CEU , awarded Torres the CEU Ángel Herrera Prize.

Established in 1997, the Herrera Prize recognizes people inside and outside the university who promote the improvement of society and the common good.

Torres’ award, which he will receive Jan. 18, 2027, was within the category of the dissemination of Catholic culture.

A statement highlighted Torres’ “contribution to the visibility of the Catholic faith from elite sport, as well as his ability to transmit Christian values ​​naturally and coherently to millions of people.”

“I’ve never tried to convey anything extraordinary,” Torres said upon receiving news the prize would go to him. “I simply to be myself,” the soccer star said, “and remain true to the values ​​that have guided me since childhood.”

“The fact that this can have a positive impact on others is something that makes me especially happy,” the Paris Saint-Germain striker added.

The jury that awarded him the prize praised Torres for “giving visibility to the Catholic faith from one of the areas with the greatest projection and influence in today’s society.”

During the World Cup, Torres was vocal about his faith and the inspiration it gave him throughout his soccer career.

After he scored the winning goal against Argentina in the dying embers of the final, he gave thanks to God. Throughout the tournament, he faced…

items.title: The day St. Peter’s Basilica hosted its first council
items.summary:
On the morning of December 8, the feast of the Immaculate Conception, torrential rain makes the streets of Rome nearly impassable. Yet even before the first cold light of dawn, a feverish excitement takes hold around St. Peter’s Basilica. “A multitude of pilgrims from every nation have come to join the Romans in welcoming the Council on its opening day,” observes Father Léon Dehon, a French priest with a journalist’s instincts who is among the crowd. The rain has not prevented the 744 council fathers from gathering in a chapel above the basilica’s vast atrium, specially prepared for the occasion. They include cardinals, bishops, and abbots from East and West, as well as vicars apostolic from distant lands such as Siam, South Africa, and China. Outside, the faithful wade through the mud. items.title: Our review: The Story of St. John Henry Newman
items.summary:
The latest film from Lumine Studios, Lead Kindly Light: The Story of Saint John Henry Newman, brings to life the rich history of Newman’s formative years and exactly what he endured for truth, beauty, and goodness, which brought about a movement that still shines today in England and the world. Directors Gustavo Letie and Julia Sondermann have done a marvelous job of bringing Newman’s early writings to life, particularly those about his path toward God and eventually the Catholic Church. They walk in the steps of Newman at his favorite place in all the world: Oxford. The film was shot across multiple countries and with multiple theologians, to give various perspectives of Newman’s journey. It shares his famous 1833 hymn/poem, “Lead, Kindly Light amid the encircling gloom,” for which the film is named, as the tipping point to Catholicism. What many people perhaps do not realize is what Newman sacrificed on his path to God Read More…

items.title: Apple’s Emmy-winning ad celebrates the joy of being ordinary
items.summary:
There are certain things that every university student should be entitled to: falling hopelessly in love with someone who barely knows they exist, going to parties they might regret the next morning, and occasionally sleeping through a lecture because of that party. And, of course, the right to be spectacularly unimpressive from time to time, to fade into the crowd and bask in the joy of being completely and utterly ignored. Which is why Apple’s Emmy-winning film I’m Not Remarkable is such a treat. Instead of presenting students with disabilities as inspirational heroes simply for getting through the day, it celebrates their right to be just like everybody else. And it does so with a fabulous musical number, plenty of humor, and a rather infectious sense of fun. Directed by Kim Gehrig, with original music from Tony Award-winning composer Tim Minchin, the film won the 2026 Emmy for Outstanding Commercial. Its stars aren’t professional actors Read More…

items.title: Pope Francis’s diary reveals encounters with the devil and a fight against control
items.summary:
Extracts from the private diary of Pope Francis are set to be released across the world, made from a collection of notes he made between 1992-2024.

The Private Diary of Pope Francis , edited by Francis’ longtime friend and collaborator Cardinal Victor Manuel Fernández offers insight into the former pope’s intense inner life, revealing mystical encounters with Jesus and the devil, and a battle against a desire to control. 

Written in a calendar used as a notebook, the entries begin in 1992 when Francis was auxiliary bishop of Buenos Aires, and the final entry is Aug. 18, 2024, when he was pope.

The book will be released in several languages, including English.

According to the diary, Francis had three encounters with the devil, two when he was in Buenos Aires and one following a disastrous trip to Chile in 2018 as pope.

In the first encounter, Francis recalled sitting in a car and seeing the “threatening yet seductive” gaze of the devil.

The second was in a Carmelite chapel, and Francis used a rosary and an invocation of the Virgin Mary to protect himself.

During the Chile trip, Francis came under heavy fire for his discrediting of victims of sexual abuse, and after being questioned on the flight home by journalists, he commissioned an investigation. 

“A few days after returning to Rome, I was in a meeting. I saw him and heard his voice, triumphant possessing everything. ‘Now I’ve gotten everything I wanted’,” Francis said in a Jan. 24, 2021 entry. 

“Just as I can’t forget his eyes from the previous two, in this case, I can’t forget the powerful raspiness of his…
items.t: Pope Francis’s diary reveals encounters with the devil and a fight against control

items.title: Leo XIV wants new Swiss Guard barracks to honor tradition
items.summary:
Pope Leo XIV wants the new Swiss Guard barracks to be a place where Swiss traditions are passed down. He made the point on Monday, November 23, to those overseeing the renovation of the Vatican’s military housing. Expressing his hope that construction will soon begin, he thanked those who have worked for years on a project intended to serve future generations. Established in 2016, the Foundation for the Renovation of the Barracks of the Pontifical Swiss Guard is responsible for a massive project to rebuild the housing and infrastructure used by the Pope’s soldiers. The current barracks, built in the 19th century, are in poor condition. In recent years, the foundation has focused on raising the funds needed for the work. items.title: Science has good news for the faithful as they age!
items.summary:
Your average churchgoing grandmother could probably tell you a thing or two about the benefits of faith in old age. But now scientists have decided to investigate the matter, and it turns out Granny might have been onto something all along. Does faith help us enjoy a happier old age? Well, according to new research, it certainly seems to be associated with a better quality of life. And while Granny might be tempted to give the scientists a knowing smile, the findings are genuinely interesting, especially as more of us are living longer. Researchers from the University of Padua in Italy examined 21 studies involving 5,664 people aged between 60 and 104, looking at the relationship between religious or spiritual beliefs and wellbeing. Their findings, published in PLOS Aging and Health and reported by CNN, revealed a positive association between faith and quality of life, as well as overall life satisfaction. The next step in her process to being declared a saint is for two miracles to be confirmed through her intercession. She joins an ever-growing group of young people who have died in the 21st century and who are being considered for canonization. items.title: Did Pope Francis experience a dark night of the soul?

Cardinal Victor Manuel Fernández, who compiled and commented on journal entries written by the Argentine pope between 1992 and 2024, describes a period of profound temptation. items.title: A vast medieval church emerges from the Sudanese desert
items.summary:
A Sudanese-Polish archaeological team has reached the original floor of what may be the largest church ever built in medieval Christian Africa, uncovering a monumental staircase in the process and raising new questions about the religious geography of a kingdom most of the world has forgotten. The structure, known as the Great Church of Jesus, sits at Old Dongola in northern Sudan — once the capital of the Kingdom of Makuria, a Christian civilization that flourished on the Nile from roughly the 6th century until the 14th. Arabic medieval sources had already identified this building as the largest and wealthiest church in all of Nubia. What archaeologists lacked, until now, was the floor to prove it. Makuria’s Christianity was not a marginal faith. The kingdom converted in the 6th century, likely through Byzantine missionaries, and went on to build churches, monasteries, and monumental public architecture across a desert that the rest of the Christian world Read More…

items.title: Kids already ask AI about God: Here is the question to teach them
items.summary:
A question about God once traveled a short distance. It went to a parent across the dinner table, to a teacher after the bell had rung, to a priest in a parish office on a weekday afternoon. It now travels to a phone at 11 at night and returns in rather less than four seconds, courteous, articulate, and apparently complete. The distance has changed, and so has what happens along the way. The two responses I hear most often from Catholics are of limited use to anyone. One treats the technology as a contagion to be kept from the young. The other treats it as a wonder and leaves the matter there. Neither is much help to a mother whose daughter asked her question hours ago and has had her answer ever since. This time of year lends itself to quiet reflection, and as we prepare for the great feast of Christmas, many people love to read a good devotional. There are lots of excellent Advent devotionals out there, but this year, we found one that’s a little different — and a lot more immersive. It’s called Way of the Star, a Catholic Advent devotional that brings together Scripture, music, and art for a prayer encounter that engages the senses and imagination.  The devotional began as a live music event through the Vigil Project, a collective of professional Catholic musicians dedicated to helping the Church encounter God through beauty. It proved so popular that the Vigil Project turned the event into a music album by the same name. As the album and live event spread around the world, “We were seeing such consistent grace,” said Andrea Thomas, co-director of The Vigil Project and co-author of Way of the Read More… 

‘Way of the Star’: An Advent devotional to hear, see, and pray

items.title: University of Dayton opens annual international Nativity display
items.summary:
You may not be setting up your Nativity scene just yet, but the University of Dayton’s beloved display of crèches from around the world opened its doors on November 16. The Catholic university’s annual exhibit of Nativity scenes from the large collection held by its Marian Library will run through January 15, and if you’re within driving distance (or visiting the area around the holidays) you don’t want to miss it. This year’s display, titled “It Takes a Village: Christmas in Community,” highlights Nativity scenes from many times and places that widen the scene beyond the stable. As the Dayton Daily News reports: “Usually, Nativity sets include Jesus, Mary, Joseph, shepherds, Magi, and animals such as sheep, donkeys and oxen,” said Bridget Retzloff, coordinator of art collections and exhibits at the Marian Library. “This year’s exhibit features Nativity sets with large village scenes, incorporating figures beyond the usual cast of characters. items.title: Pope appeals for peace on Christ the King, dines with Rome’s poor
items.summary:
Pope Leo XIV renewed his appeal for peace around the globe on Sunday, calling on leaders in positions of responsibility to work for equitable solutions to conflicts.

Addressing pilgrims and tourists in St. Peter’s Square for the Angelus on Sunday, the pontiff called the faithful to prayer “for the victims of the many conflicts that, sadly, continue to sow death and suffering throughout the world.”

“Let us pray for those in positions of responsibility,” Leo also said, “that they may commit to finding solutions for reconciliation and peace without delay.”

Pope Leo XIV greets pilgrims and tourists from the window of the Apostolic Palace in the Vatican on Sunday, 22 Nov. 2026. Image ©Vatican Media 

Peace has been a key motif of Leo’s pontificate, and he has prayed for an end to armed conflict in many of the world’s trouble spots, but his appeal this Sunday was global in scope and came on the Solemnity of Christ the King.

In remarks ahead of the traditional noonday Marian devotion, Leo recalled the intention of his predecessor, Pope Pius XI, who established the feast day in 1925, as the world slowly recovered from the horror of World War I.

“ In an era marked by tensions and conflicts,” Leo said, “my predecessor wished to emphasize that the Lord of history is the King of peace and justice for all the peoples of the world.”

“As a pilgrim through the centuries,” the pontiff also said, “the Church renews this teaching, proclaiming that the Kingdom of God is coming and will endure forever.”

Following the Angelus prayer on Sunday, the pope also prayed for young people…
items.t: Pope appeals for peace on Christ the King, dines with Rome’s poor families

items.title: Pope appeals for aid as ‘Super El Niño’ drives severe weather conditions across Asia-Pacific
items.summary:
Pope Leo XIV appealed for those suffering from a severe drought across Asia and Oceania, as emergency aid workers continue their work to alleviate conditions of food insecurity and economic hardship.

The U.N.’s Office of Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs says the El Niño-driven conditions could compound existing vulnerabilities across vast swathes of the Asia-Pacific region.

OCHA says as many as 190 million children face heightened risks to food and water security, general nutrition and health, as well as shelter, and education.

“My thoughts and prayers go out to the people of Papua New Guinea and other Pacific countries affected by drought,” the pontiff said Sunday after praying the Angelus with pilgrims and tourists gathered in St. Peter’s Square.

All 22 provinces of Papua New Guinea are currently facing emergency drought conditions, while experts are warning that this year’s El Niño phenomenon is driving severe weather across Asia and the Pacific.

The pope expressed his “closeness to all those suffering as a result of this emergency,” and offered his “gratitude to those working to assist the most severely affected.”

The U.N.’s Food and Agriculture Organization participated in an emergency meeting for Papua New Guinea in late October.

Earlier this month the OCHA issued a forecast saying experts expect humanitarian impacts to unfold in three successive waves over the next six months.

Weather experts say this year’s “Super El Niño” effect driving both drought and severe storm activity.

items.title: There’s probably a cult hiding in plain sight on your high street. At last, Britain is confronting the problem | Rachael Reign
items.summary:
As MPs discuss the menace of ‘high-control religious groups’, I welcome the political attention – but survivors of this abuse deserve real action

  • Rachael Reign is the founder of Surviving Universal UK

Britain is confronting its cult problem. Better late than never.

They don’t advertise themselves as cults. They don’t register as cults. And they certainly don’t have the word above the door. But make no mistake: cults operate in communities across Britain. Chances are, there’s one on your local high street.

Rachael Reign is the founder of Surviving Universal UK

In the UK, the charity Mind is available on 0300 123 3393 and Childline on 0800 1111. In the US, call or text Mental Health America at 988 or chat 988lifeline.org. In Australia, support is available at Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, Lifeline on 13 11 14, and at MensLine on 1300 789 978. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org.

items.title: Fred Nile, former NSW politician and figurehead of the rightwing Christian Democratic party, dies aged 92
items.summary:
Controversial figure frequently took positions against drug use, abortion and homosexuality, but in later years supported legislation expunging homosexual convictions

  • Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

The former New South Wales MP and longstanding figurehead of the rightwing Christian Democratic party, the Rev Fred Nile, has died aged 92.

Nile was a member of the NSW legislative council for more than 40 years. He first entered the state’s upper house in 1981 and retired after unsuccessfully contesting the 2023 election.

items.title: I’m a priest. Silicon Valley’s search for the ‘soul’ of AI is deeply troubling | Rev Kevin Deal
items.summary:
Humans experience beauty and sit with mysteries. Unlike AI, we do not exist merely for utility

Last month, religious leaders from across San Francisco gathered behind closed doors to discuss what it means to be human in the age of artificial intelligence.

Anthropic, the AI company operating only a couple of miles from my parish, has been courting priests, rabbis and theologians. Its billionaire cofounder, Christopher Olah, has even pressed Vatican advisers to take seriously the possibility that his company’s chatbot might possess consciousness.

items.title: ‘Shakespearean tale of ego, greed and ambition’: the scandalous story of televangelism
items.summary:
Netflix documentary Primetime Preacher$ travels back to a time when evangelism found a dominant place on US television – and the shocking tabloid stories that followed

For three decades, film-maker Joe Berlinger has gripped true-crime buffs with his deep dives into small-town murders and infamous serial killers. His Netflix explorations of John Wayne Gacy and Jeffrey Dahmer helped flip documentary storytelling from viewer homework to a welcome distraction.

After dedicating so much time to the life of Jeffrey Epstein, the kidnapping of JonBenét Ramsey and other unsolved mysteries, Berlinger thought Primetime Preacher$, his new Netflix documentary on America’s televangelist boom, would offer a break. But it turns out that’s a pretty juicy crime story too, about the religious right’s bank job on American politics. “The deeper resonance for me came when I realized that the global televangelism rise actually mirrors the rise of the religious right,” he says. “Religion and politics, from Reagan on, has really changed politics for the worse in my opinion. This was the birth of that.”

items.t: ‘Shakespearean tale of ego, greed and ambition’: the scandalous story of televangelism
